clue.text: House-builder giving evidence_ flips his lid .

definitions.note: a verb phrase describing what the toy does, standing for the toy itself

blocks.note: in the nursery rhyme, this is the house that Jack built
a witness giving evidence stands in the witness box

explanation.surface: A builder in the witness stand loses his temper while testifying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flips his lid' looks like slang for losing one's temper, but it is literal: the toy's lid flips open and a figure springs out.
explanation.definitionFit: The toy is a box whose lid springs open to release a jumping figure on a coiled spring.

clue.text: Doorman gets rise after beginning  of the year

indicators.note: after places one piece behind another, so the hill named first in the clue comes second in the grid

blocks.note: the year begins on January 1st, written Jan I with a Roman numeral
a tor is a rocky hill, a rise in the ground

explanation.surface: A doorman is given a pay rise just after New Year.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rise' looks like a pay increase but is a hill; a tor is a rocky hilltop, especially on Dartmoor. The word itself comes from Janus, Roman god of doors, who also names January.
explanation.definitionFit: The word originally meant a doorkeeper or porter, and still names a caretaker who looks after a building's entrances.

clue.text: Show fear of an oppressor ?

blocks.note: first meaning: to crouch or shrink back in fright
second meaning: one who cows or intimidates others

explanation.surface: Someone trembles in dread before a tyrant.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the invented second sense: someone who cows people would be a cow-er.
explanation.definitionFit: To crouch in fear is the verb's usual sense; a bully who intimidates others could jokingly be called one who cows.

clue.text: Can't be right to be so tense

definitions.note: a verb phrase standing for an adjective meaning flawed

blocks.note: first meaning: flawed, not without fault
second meaning: the grammatical tense for continuing past action, as in 'I was walking'

explanation.surface: Someone frets that they cannot be correct while feeling so anxious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tense' looks like an adjective for nervousness, but it is the grammar noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Something with faults is not flawless, and grammar also names a past tense for ongoing or repeated actions this way.

clue.text: A kind character, we read

blocks.note: first meaning: a sort or category
second meaning: a printed letter, as set by a printer for us to read

explanation.surface: We learn from reading that someone is a good-natured sort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kind' reads as the adjective for generous, but it is the noun meaning sort.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means a category or sort, and also the printed letters and characters that printers set on a page.

clue.text: Could this coin be a rupee ? No

definitions.text: Could this coin be a rupee ? No

indicators.note: to coin is to invent or mint something new, so the following letters are minted into a new arrangement

blocks.note: taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a foreign coin might be a rupee, and the answer is no.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coin' looks like a noun, but read as a verb it signals the rearrangement. As a whole, the clue describes the euro, a coin of Europe that is certainly no rupee.
explanation.definitionFit: A euro is a coin belonging to Europe, so this adjective describes it, and a rupee is Indian, not from that continent.

clue.text: A man in Spain lost his head in a game

indicators.note: losing a head means the first letter is dropped from the word for the man

blocks.note: the Spanish word for man

explanation.surface: A Spanish gentleman was beheaded during some contest.
explanation.walkthrough: Dropping the silent first letter of the Spanish word leaves the name of an old card game popular in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a three-handed card game of Spanish origin, fashionable in Europe around the time of Pope's poems.

clue.text: So.important a virtue in a churchman

blocks.note: first meaning: the four principal virtues are given this name, from its sense of chief or fundamental
second meaning: a senior prelate of the Roman Catholic Church

explanation.surface: Goodness is a quality highly valued in a clergyman.
explanation.walkthrough: The four classical virtues of prudence, justice, temperance and fortitude are named this way because they are the most important.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means chief or fundamental, as in the four principal virtues, and is also the title of a senior Catholic prelate.

clue.text: Anger, rising about cricket team. Remedy this

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising means the word is read upwards, from bottom to top
about means going round, so the reversed word surrounds the team

blocks.note: to rile is to anger
a cricket team has eleven players, XI in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A cricket side's fury needs some cure.
explanation.walkthrough: RILE reversed gives ELIR, which opens after ELI to take in XI. XI for a cricket team is a crossword staple.
explanation.definitionFit: An elixir is a supposed cure-all, a magical or medicinal potion believed to heal any ailment.

clue.text: Fresh spring by which we are _daily benefited

definitions.note: a relative clause describing the thing, standing for a noun

blocks.note: fresh means new
a spa is a mineral spring
per means by, as in 'per post'

explanation.surface: Fresh water from a mineral spring does us good every day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'By' does double duty in the surface but in the wordplay is PER; the rest describes a thing that informs us each morning.
explanation.definitionFit: A daily printed publication brings readers the day's reports, which is the benefit the clue says we get each day.

clue.text: In Scotland fine many for a noisy quarrel

blocks.note: braw is the Scots word for fine or splendid
L is the Roman numeral for fifty, a large number

explanation.surface: A Scottish court imposes a heavy penalty on many people for a rowdy argument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fine' looks like a penalty, but it is the adjective meaning splendid, which in Scots is braw.
explanation.definitionFit: A brawl is a rough, rowdy fight or scuffle, usually loud and involving several people.

clue.text: Ring-fighter about to pierce his adversary's heart

indicators.note: piercing means going into something, here into the centre of the adversary

blocks.note: the bullfighter's adversary is the bull, toro in Spanish; the word goes in at its heart
re means about, concerning

explanation.surface: A boxer is on the point of landing a blow to his opponent's heart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ring' suggests boxing, but the ring is a bullring; a bull in Spanish is TORO, and RE goes into its middle.
explanation.definitionFit: A torero is a bullfighter, especially one on foot, who fights the bull in the arena.

clue.text: Literary supplement anybody can do without.

blocks.note: first meaning: extra material added at the end of a book
second meaning: a small organ in the gut that people live perfectly well without

explanation.surface: A literary magazine's supplement is something no reader needs.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface sounds like a sneer at a book review section; the second part is the vestigial organ often removed by surgery.
explanation.definitionFit: Supplementary material at the back of a book shares its name with the vestigial organ attached to the large intestine.

clue.text: Cause of friction Mrs Battle enjoyed

blocks.note: first meaning: anything that rubs
second meaning: Sarah Battle, in Charles Lamb's essay, loved a game of whist, played in sets of games with this name

explanation.surface: A quarrelsome woman relished stirring up conflict.
explanation.walkthrough: Mrs Battle is the whist-loving old lady of Charles Lamb's essay 'Mrs Battle's Opinions on Whist'; a set of games at whist or bridge has this name.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that rubs creates friction, and in card games such as whist and bridge a match of three games is called this.

clue.text: Weapons used by English in Burns's version

indicators.note: a version is a different rendering of something, so the letters are recast

blocks.note: Eng is the abbreviation for English
taken as written

explanation.surface: Arms carried by the English appear in a poem by Robert Burns.
explanation.walkthrough: The name of Scotland's national poet suggests a literary clue, but his name is just letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: These were light machine guns used by British forces from the 1930s, so they are firearms or weapons.

clue.text: Sporting gentleman?_

blocks.note: surface reading: a man fond of field sports, or one who plays fair
setter's reading: the man who flies a hawk, the female peregrine being called a falcon-gentle

explanation.walkthrough: Hawking was a gentleman's sport, and falconers called a trained female peregrine a 'falcon gentle'.
explanation.definitionFit: The man trains and flies hunting birds, an aristocratic field sport practised for centuries by gentlemen.

clue.text: Mrs Mopp meets the king in Belgium

definitions.note: a phrase standing for a place in Belgium

blocks.note: Mrs Mopp was the charlady in the wartime radio comedy ITMA; a char is a cleaning woman
le roi is French for the king, French being spoken in southern Belgium

explanation.surface: A cleaning lady has an audience with the Belgian monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: A char or charlady is a British word for a cleaning woman; Mrs Mopp was a famous one from the radio show ITMA.
explanation.definitionFit: Charleroi is an industrial city in the French-speaking Wallonia region of southern Belgium.

clue.text: D-Day exercise _would be useless if standing order ignored

indicators.note: ignoring something means leaving it out, so those letters are dropped from the answer

blocks.note: in vain means to no purpose, useless
SO is the banking abbreviation for a standing order

explanation.surface: A military operation fails because the regular orders were disregarded.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay runs backwards: take the S and the O out of the answer and what is left reads IN VAIN. A standing order is an instruction to a bank to pay a fixed sum regularly.
explanation.definitionFit: D-Day in June 1944 was the Allied landing in Normandy, an armed incursion into occupied France.

clue.text: Giving tongue like Malory's beast

blocks.note: first meaning: of hounds, baying while searching for a scent
second meaning: in Malory's Arthurian tales, King Pellinore pursues a creature with this name

explanation.surface: Someone speaks up, roaring like a creature from Arthurian legend.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur features the Questing Beast, whose belly made a noise like hounds baying.
explanation.definitionFit: Hunting hounds searching for game are said to be at work in this way when they bay, and Malory's elusive creature bears that name.

clue.text: Measures said to be used for this time control

definitions.note: a phrase describing what the mineral is used for

indicators.note: said means spoken, so we want the word that sounds like the measures

blocks.note: quarts are liquid measures of two pints

explanation.surface: Units of measurement are reportedly used for regulating time.
explanation.walkthrough: A quart is a quarter of a gallon. The crystal it sounds like vibrates at a steady frequency and keeps many watches accurate.
explanation.definitionFit: Clocks and watches regulated by a vibrating crystal of this mineral are named after it, so it governs timekeeping.

clue.text: Dubious cigar, about a pound, has a strong smell

definitions.note: a verb phrase describing the bulb, standing for it

indicators.note: something dubious is suspect and not to be taken as it stands, so its letters are rearranged
about means around, so the rearranged word goes round the unit of weight

blocks.note: taken letter for letter
L is the abbreviation for pound, from Latin libra

explanation.surface: A suspect cigar weighing around a pound gives off a powerful odour.
explanation.definitionFit: The bulb used in cooking is famous for its pungent odour that lingers on the breath.

clue.text: Indian manoeuvre on ice

blocks.note: first meaning: a member of a Native American people of the south-eastern United States
second meaning: a figure-skating step from one edge to the opposite edge

explanation.surface: A Native American performs a move while skating.
explanation.walkthrough: In figure skating, this is a step changing foot and edge and direction, named after the people, as is the related Mohawk.
explanation.definitionFit: The name belongs to a Native American nation and also to a figure-skating step, as the Mohawk does too.

clue.text: 31 days, if even more years in this golden age

definitions.note: a noun phrase standing for an adjective describing that age

blocks.note: a month of 31 days
an is an archaic word for if, as in Shakespeare's 'an it please you'

explanation.surface: A month with even more years in it would be a golden era.
explanation.walkthrough: Several months have 31 days; the one named after the emperor Augustus fits here. 'If' as the archaic AN is an old convention.
explanation.definitionFit: The reign of Augustus was the classic peak of Latin literature, so the adjective describes any similar peak of refined writing.

clue.text: Second journey by river

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for second
a tour is a journey

explanation.surface: A second trip is made along a river.
explanation.walkthrough: Several English rivers bear this name, including ones in Dorset, Kent and Suffolk.
explanation.definitionFit: The name belongs to several rivers in southern and eastern England, such as the one painted by Constable.

clue.text: What' is woven by love or fate

blocks.note: cloth is a woven material
love is zero in tennis, which looks like O

explanation.surface: Someone wonders what fabric is spun by love or destiny.
explanation.walkthrough: In Greek myth there are three Fates: one spins the thread of life, one measures it and one cuts it. The spinner fits the weaving surface neatly.
explanation.definitionFit: She is one of the three Greek Fates, the spinner of the thread of each human life.

clue.text: The sort of person he is

definitions.text: The sort of person he is

blocks.clueFragment: The sort of person he is
blocks.note: surface reading: a remark about someone's character
setter's reading: in grammar, 'he' belongs to a numbered person, after I and you

explanation.walkthrough: Grammar ranks pronouns by person: I is first, you is second, and he, she and it come next.
explanation.definitionFit: Grammatical person counts I as first and you as second, so the pronoun he belongs to the next one in order.

clue.text: YMCA here in USA?

blocks.note: surface reading: where a Young Men's Christian Association hostel might be found in America
setter's reading: Young Men's Christian Association recast as Brigham Young's Mormon church, which settled this state

explanation.walkthrough: Brigham Young led the Mormons, members of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, to found Salt Lake City; the initials are read as a Young Mormon Church Association.
explanation.definitionFit: The western American state was settled by Mormon pioneers led by Brigham Young, and the church still has its headquarters there.

clue.text: Get browned off and leave the dance

blocks.note: to tan is to get brown in the sun
to go is to leave

explanation.surface: Someone fed up storms out of a ball.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Browned off' is British slang for fed up, but the phrase splits: 'get browned' is the wordplay and 'off' only joins it to the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a ballroom dance of Argentine origin, danced by couples with sharp, dramatic movements.

clue.text: Prohibit cider-manufacturer entering in race

indicators.note: a manufacturer makes something new out of raw material, so those letters are refashioned
entering means going inside, so the remade letters go into the race

blocks.note: taken as written
taken letter for letter
the TT, or Tourist Trophy, is the motorcycle race on the Isle of Man

explanation.surface: A drinks firm is banned from sponsoring a race.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphen joins 'cider' and 'manufacturer' as one company in the surface, but the second word only tells you to rework the first.
explanation.definitionFit: To interdict is to forbid or ban by authority, a formal, legal and ecclesiastical word for prohibition.

clue.text: Nice outlook?

blocks.note: surface reading: a pleasant view or a cheerful prospect
setter's reading: Nice the city on the Riviera, so a view from a house in that country

explanation.walkthrough: The capital letter is hidden at the start: Nice is the French Riviera city, and an outlook is something you look out of.
explanation.definitionFit: A pair of glazed doors opening onto a garden or balcony is called this, and from Nice you would look out through one.
